3153.dq: 基本的に語末から二音節目にストレスが置かれる。…語末が子音の場合は、語末から数えて一音節目にストレスが置かれる。 (positions counted from 語末 'word end'; examples are single words: 〔βi=já=e〕‘tree’, 〔βi=tu=βo=βó=ra〕‘star’, 〔nen=to=βón〕‘now’, 〔láŋ〕‘wind’)
3153.dloc: Naito 2003, §5 アクセント, p.150; Q&A p.152, Mitani's remark on stress vs pitch accent. Naito 2008 degree abstract p.1515 (p.1, paragraph on 第２章).
3153.heavy: 語末が子音の場合 'when the word ends in a consonant' — i.e. a closed (CVC) final syllable attracts stress; permitted codas are /β r l/ and nasals (§4). No phonemic vowel length (5 vowels; lengthening is a phonetic effect of stress), so only coda closure counts.
3153.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word as the default; when the word ends in a consonant (closed final syllable: codas β r l or a nasal), stress falls on the final syllable. Stressed vowels are pronounced strongly and tend to lengthen.
3153.srule: Not mentioned in Naito 2003, §5 アクセント p.150 (whole accent section read; every example, including five-syllable 〔βi=tu=βo=βó=ra〕 'star', carries a single stress mark); the Naito 2008 thesis abstract (p.1515) is likewise silent.
3153.quote: Naito 2003, p.150, §5 アクセント: 「Tutuba語はアクセント言語であると考えられ、基本的に語末から二音節目にストレスが置かれる。ストレスが置かれる箇所は強く発音され、長母音化する傾向にある。〔βi=já=e〕‘tree’ 〔βi=tu=βo=βó=ra〕‘star’ 語末が子音の場合は、語末から数えて一音節目にストレスが置かれる。〔nen=to=βón〕‘now’ 〔láŋ〕‘wind’」 [= Tutuba is considered an accent language; stress is basically placed on the second syllable from the end of the word. The stressed position is pronounced strongly and tends to lengthen its vowel. When the word ends in a consonant, stress is placed on the first syllable counting from the end.] ... p.152 (Q&A, 三谷): 「アクセントに関して、発表者はこの言語がストレスアクセントではなく、ピッチアクセントの可能性もあると悩んでいたようだが、仮にピッチアクセントであ…
3153.loc: Naito 2003, §5 アクセント, p.150; Q&A p.152, Mitani's remark on stress vs pitch accent. Naito 2008 degree abstract p.1515 (p.1, paragraph on 第２章).
3153.idn: Tutuba語 — the language of Tutuba Island, Republic of Vanuatu, used by about 500 people; no dialect named (the paper compares generations: speakers in their 70s vs 30s).; data: Author's own fieldwork on Tutuba Island, Vanuatu: recordings made in 2002 of informants in their 70s and 30s…
3153.exq_: 基本的に語末から二音節目にストレスが置かれる。 (the only hedge is 基本的に 'basically'; no exceptions are enumerated; the 2008 abstract repeats the same hedge: アクセントはストレス型で，基本的に語末から二音節目の母音に置かれる)
3153.tone: Not tonal. Naito had considered a pitch-accent analysis; in the printed discussion (p.152) Mitani states that a pitch accent would show a higher, emphasised pitch on the accented syllable and that from the tapes 'there is no doubt it is stress accent' (ストレスアクセントであることは間違いない). The 2008 abstract likewise says アクセントはストレス型.

[the 'forms' are single verb words; the same page separately notes phrase-level enclisis: na/dit/t!ō is …
3154.prule: No positional word-stress rule: Sapir reports that stress accent is 'not particularly well marked'; syllables are roughly equal in prominence ('approximately level accentual flow with but few peaks'); accents he transcribed after long-vowel prefixes are reinterpreted as level stress on syllables 1-2. The 1914 source neither gives a stress position nor a weight condition; it stops short of Morice's 'no accent' but describes no word-stress system.
3154.srule: No secondary-stress rule. Sapir's only mention of secondary accent: two trisyllabic verb forms he had written with an accent on the second syllable after a long prefix vowel (nā/dít/t!ō, tc!ā/θíl/se) 'might perhaps better be written nå/dìt/t!ō and tc!å/θìl/se with secondary accent on second syllable', i.e. level stress over syllables 1-2, within a word accent he describes as weak and level ('few peaks').
3154.quote: In general, however, stress accent cannot be said to be particularly well marked in Chasta Costa.⁷ Each syllable is a fairly well-defined phonetic unit tending to hold its own against others, so that an approximately level accentual flow with but few peaks results. 3155.dq: Dans un mot polysyllabique prononcé isolément, il y a toujours une syllabe qui est mise en valeur par un accent expiratoire ... Dans un texte suivi où s'établit une hiérarchie des mots, il se forme des groupes de mots reliés par un seul accent — certains mots perdent l'accent qu'ils portent à l'état isolé.
3155.dloc: Introduction phonologique, section 'L'accent', pp. 31-33; deciding statement p. 32, continuation and fixed/mobile accent classes p. 33
3155.prule: Word stress (a weak expiratory accent, one per polysyllabic word in isolation) is lexically specified: 'nothing allows one to predict the place of the accent in a given word; all syllables can bear the accent'. Very low functional load; a handful of minimal pairs (asán 'it rots' vs ásan 'he sells it', sə́qʷa 'my son' vs səqʷá 'I am a son', etc.).
3155.srule: Only at phrase level: in connected speech words form accent groups under a single accent, some losing their isolation accent, and 'un faible accent secondaire' appears within such groups (yàdan áč'). No word-internal secondary stress: the isolated polysyllable has one weak expiratory accent, and Vogt regards Mészáros's (1934) systematic marking of a secondary accent as unmotivated ('on ne voit guère pourquoi').
3155.quote: Les conclusions auxquelles nous sommes arrivé, sont les suivantes: Dans un mot polysyllabique prononcé isolément, il y a toujours une syllabe qui est mise en valeur par un accent expiratoire, relativement faible et souvent difficile à saisir. Les informateurs eux-mêmes n'en semblent pas conscients, et y paient en tout cas peu d'attention ... Les cas où un informateur averti comme Tevfik Esenç de lui-même signale une différenciation par l'accent sont exceptionnels; l'on constate, en effet, que le cas se présente rarement. ... L'accent a en tout cas un rendement fonctionnel très modeste. ... Ri…
3155.loc: Introduction phonologique, section 'L'accent', pp. 31-33; deciding statement p. 32, continuation and fixed/mobile accent classes p. 33

[For the mobile-class secondary rule, p. 33] Quelques mots dissyllabiques accentuées sur la finale reportent l'accent non sur l'article mais sur la première syllabe, łapqə́ race (mot composé …
3155.tone: No tone system. Vogt p. 32: stressed syllables generally have a higher pitch than unstressed ones except phrase-finally before a pause (falling tone); in rising-intonation interrogatives the final syllable carries the high pitch while the first carries the expiratory accent ('il peut y avoir désaccord entre accent expiratoire et ton musical').
3155.sec_quote: Dans un texte suivi où s'établit une hiérarchie des mots, il se forme des groupes de mots reliés par un seul accent — certains mots perdent l'accent qu'ils portent à l'état isolé. [...] L'apparition d'un faible accent secondaire dans ses groupes, par ex. yàdan áč' est certainement responsable d'une partie des contracdictions dans la notation de l'accent, de texte à texte, d'auteur à auteur.
3155.sec_loc: Introduction phonologique, 'L'accent', p. 32; remark on Mészáros p. 31

secx.sec_quote_tr: In a connected text, where a hierarchy of words is established, groups of words linked by a single accent are formed — some words lose the accent they carry in isolation. [...] The appearance of a weak secondary accent in these groups, e.g. yàdan áč', is certainly responsible for part of the contradictions in the notation of the accent from text to text and from author to author.

3157.dq: The phonological word is defined as the rank whose unit functions in the intonation group and whose structure is stated in terms of syllables. The phonological word in Gong may have up to four syllables. It has one stressed syllable which always occupies the last position of a word as its nucleus, and it may have weakly stressed or unstressed syllables as its periphery.
3157.dloc: Mayuree 2006, ch. V sec. 5.1.2 'Phonological word', pp. 95-97; lit. review p. 21; p. 100. Pusit 1986, sec. 2.2-2.3.1 pp. 16-17; sec. 2.3.2.4 'Stress in verbs' p. 23; conclusions 5.1.1.
3157.prule: Fixed final: the single strongly stressed syllable is always the last syllable of the phonological word (the 'major syllable'); words have 1-4 syllables.
3157.srule: Weak (secondary-degree) stress, non-rhythmic, placed by syllable type: apart from the single strong stress on the final 'major syllable', a non-final full 'minor syllable' carries weak stress and a reduced 'presyllable' (open Ca33) carries none; attested shapes u.s, w.s, w.u.s, u.w.s, u.w.u.s (at most one weak stress per word, initial or second depending on where the minor syllable sits). No alternating/rhythmic secondary stress is described.

3157.tone: Gong is tonal. Mayuree 2006's own analysis (Kok Chiang dialect) has FOUR tonemes: ch. V sec. 5.1.4.3 'The tones function as the nucleus in the syllable. There are four tones in Gong.' (low [21], mid [31, 33], low rising [24, 231, 241, 251], high falling [42]); orthography chapter 'There are four tonemes in Kok Chiang Gong: low, mid, low-rising, and high-falling.'; conclusions p. 156 'four tonemes: mid, low, low-rising, high-falling'. The five-tone list on p. 21 ('high level, low level, mid level, low-rising, and high-falling') is the literature-review summary of Pusit (1986) for the Khok Khwai (Uthai Thani) dialect (p. 20: 'Pusit (1986) studied the phonology of Ugong in Uthaithani province'), not Mayuree's Kok Chiang analysis. Tone sandhi occurs in di-/trisyllabic compounds (5.1.4.4.3.6). Mayuree 2007, Bradley 1992 and Bradley 2023 describe tones and sandhi without mentioning stress. Stress is described as a positional word-level property separate from tone. Pusit 1986 (sec. 2.2.3): unstressed syllables 'can have only 4 vowels (i, ə, a, u) and can bear only Tone 2'; Mayuree 2006 p. 100: 'Only vowels /i, a, u/ can occur in open unstressed syllables.'

3158.dq: There are no right-edge factors such as assignment of H boundary tones, nor is there an attraction to a strong (e.g. stressed) or weak (e.g. unstressed) position.
3158.dloc: sec. 2.5 'Essential grammar background', sub-headings 'Tones' and 'Syllable structure and minimal word', pp. 55-56; sec. 3.2.1 'The TBU in Ikaan', p. 86; sec. 7.6.1, p. 339
3158.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Ikaan is described as a two-tone language (H, L) with downstep of H after a floating L; the mora is the tone-bearing unit and each mora bears one tone; surface contours are tone clusters; syllables are V, CV, CVC with long or short V; the minimal word is bimoraic. Stress/accent is not a parameter of the description; the one stress-related remark (p. 339) denies that leftward H copying is attracted to a strong (stressed) or prominent position.

As all following chapters in this thesis are concerned with tone, no further information will be given here. [p. 56] Possible syllable structures in Ikaan are V, CV and CVC. In all three types, V can be either long or short. ... The minimal word in Ikaan is bimoraic. Since most Ikaan words consist of a root prefixed with a vowel they automatically have two moras. 3158.loc: sec. 2.5 'Essential grammar background', sub-headings 'Tones' and 'Syllable structure and minimal word', pp. 55-56; sec. 3.2.1 'The TBU in Ikaan', p. 86; sec. 7.6.1, p. 339
3158.idn: The cited thesis describes Ikaan, one dialect of Ukaan, as spoken in the Ikakumo villages (Ondo and Edo States); the other Ukaan lects (Ise/Ishe, Auga, Ayanran) are not described. Glottolog ukaa1243 covers the whole Ukaan cluster.
3158.tone: Two-tone system: 'There are two tones in Ikaan, a high tone (H) and a low tone (L). After floating L, H is downstepped.' (p. 55). TBU = mora: sec. 3.2.1 (p. 86) argues for the mora as TBU and sec. 3.3.4 restates 'the mora is the TBU... each mora can bear only one tone'; falling and rising surface contours are 'sequences of level tones underlyingly, i.e. tonal clusters rather than true contour tones'. Tone is lexical and grammatical (minimal pairs, tonal inflection). The thesis mentions 'stress' only twice (p. 28, non-linguistic use; p. 339) and 'prominent' only at p. 339 (denied as the target of leftward copying) and in sentence-level polar-question prosody (register expansion, breathy termination). No stress or pitch-accent rule is given; the description is silent on word stress rather than explicitly denying it. Corroborated in the saved Salffner 2017 (LabPhon 8(1):14, sec. 2, p. 5: 'Ikaan is a tone language... There are two underlying tones, a high tone (H) and a low tone (L).') and Salffner 2015 (LD&C 9, p. 240: 'a two-tone-plus-downstep system'), neither of which mentions word stress.

Connell 1994 (JWAL 24(1), sec. 3.3 p.10 and sec. 5 p.12) repeats: two tones H/L + contrastive downstep in all languages of the group; tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.'

3164.dq: Word accent is usually morphologically conditioned, with accent falling on the first syllable of the root, which may be, but is not necessarily, the first syllable of the word.
3164.prule: Word accent on the first syllable of the ROOT (morphologically conditioned, as in Standard German); the root-initial syllable is usually but not necessarily word-initial (unstressed prefixes precede it); morphologically conditioned deviations (phrasal verbs) pattern as in Standard German; words of non-German origin keep the accent of their source language; hence 'typologically free' (any syllable possible), not a weight rule.

3165.prule: Germanic root/stem stress as in Standard German: main stress falls on the stem syllable of native words (surfacing as initial or penultimate stress in native roots); unstressed prefixes (ge-, ver-, be-) and inflectional/derivational endings are unstressed and reduced; compounds carry main stress on the first member and secondary stress on the second; borrowed and polymorphemic words can show other patterns.
3165.srule: Only in compounds: Hauptton on the first member, Nebenton (secondary stress) on the second, except words compounded with an inseparable particle (Goepfert 1878: 63, West Erzgebirgisch). Not mentioned in Khan & Weise 2013 (p. 238 'Stress'; their transcriptions pp. 231-239 carry no secondary-stress marks, compounds such as Nordwind, Sonnenstrahlen bear only the primary mark on the first member). No word-level rhythmic secondary stress described in any source read (Khan & Weise 2013; Franke 1884 sections 7, 65; Goepfert 1878 pp. 20-21, 63; Albrecht 1881 section 149; Kuegler 2005 sections 2.2.2, 5.1).

3166.prule: Final (main-syllable) stress. Prosodic words are at most disyllabic iambs: an optional presyllable, which is always unstressed and phonotactically reduced, plus the word-final main syllable, which is always prosodically prominent; monosyllables are bare main syllables. Position depends only on the syllable count (last syllable), not on weight.

3167.dq: Described in this section are the major prosodic patterns observed in utterances consisting of simple declarative clauses ending in a verb. ... This pattern of gently declining pitch with very slight stem stress is very common in the Tetlin dialect, where there is no low tone.

3167.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Upper Tanana is described as a tone language (unmarked vs. low-marked vs. high-marked syllables; Lovick 2020: 72). 3167.tone: Lovick 2020: 72: 'Upper Tanana is a tone language distinguishing unmarked, low-marked, and high-marked syllables.' Sec. 7.2: 'The Northway, Scottie Creek, and Beaver Creek dialects of Upper Tanana have lexical low tone caused by suprasegmentalization of a historical glottal segment in the syllable rhyme... 3168.prule: One culminative high pitch (f0 peak) per morpheme, marked with an acute; in nouns it is confined to a right-edge window of the last two syllables. In citation form or as subject, most nouns carry the high pitch on the final syllable (Subject-pattern A) and a lexically marked minority on the penult (Subject-pattern B); when the same nouns are objects the two classes swap (A -> penult, B -> final). Object nouns belong to four lexically specified groups that place the high pitch of the following verb on its initial, second or final syllable, or leave the verb with no high pitch. Placement is blind to vowel length. The authors explicitly decline to classify the system as stress, tone or pitch accent and report no evidence of tonal contrast.

No source states a word-stress rule; the culminative single-H system with a lexically classed, syntactically conditioned position is coded tone or pitch accent.

3171.dq: Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word. ... On the surface, then, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of nouns bearing the enclitic =a.
3171.dloc: dos Santos 2024, ch. 3 sec. 3.2.1 'Sound inventory, phonotactics and stress': stress paragraph and exx. (7)-(13) p. 40; exx. (14)-(16) p. 41 (page numbers are running heads at page top). Scope statement sec. 3.2 'based on the Juma and Jupaú dialects' p. 34. Nasal-vowel/stress remark ('which coincides with the location of stress') p. 37. Sec. 3.2.3.1 'Nasal post-oralization' with the primary-stress diacritic sentence p. 42. Diminutive /-ʔi/ as the only glottal-stop-initial morpheme, p. 40. Identity: abbreviation list 'uRz iso code for Jupaú (also known as Uru Eu Wau Wau)'.
3171.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the lexical root ('the root-final syllable of a word'). The obligatory nominalizing enclitic =a is extrametrical, so surface nouns are penultimate-stressed ([ñã.ˈndu.a], [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa]) while bare verb forms are final-stressed ([ɛ.ˈpi], [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi]); the negation circumfix nd(a)-...-i leaves stress on the root ([nd-aĩˈmbɛ-i]); a listed set of suffixes (-ahim 'very', -uhu 'aug', -ʔi 'dim') attract stress onto themselves ([aĩmbɛ-aˈhĩm], [j-ipi-uˈhu], [vɨɾaˈʔia]). Position is therefore set by morpheme identity (root vs. extrametrical clitic/affix vs. stress-attracting suffix), not by syllable count from a word edge and not by syllable weight.
3171.srule: Not mentioned in dos Santos 2024 (ch. 3 sec. 3.2 'Phonology and writing system', pp. 34-51 read; sec. 3.2.1 pp. 40-41 gives the primary rule only, and p. 42 states 'I indicate primary stress in phonological rules and examples with the diacritic (ˈ)' with no statement on secondary or rhythmic stress anywhere in the work).

3172.prule: Stress in all content words is dynamic (expiratory) and falls on the last syllable of the word; particles, postpositions and the negation affix are the only unstressed elements, so stress precedes the negation suffix (almá 'apple' vs. álma 'don't take').
3172.srule: A word extended by a series of affixes may carry two stresses (only example: менė́мҗäсėнä́ 'in my opinion', accents on the 2nd and the final syllable); where the non-final stress falls is not stated.
3172.quote: Ударение во всех знаменательных словах является силовым и падает на последний слог слова. Неударными являются лишь частицы, послелоги, аффикс отрицания. В силу этого в ряде случаев ударение играет фонематическую роль, ср.: алма́ ‘яблоко’, и а́лма ‘не бери’. 3173.dq: La raíz de una palabra es la sílaba que lleva el acento fonético (la sílaba que lleva mayor fuerza o énfasis). A la raíz son añadidos los prefijos o sufijos necesarios.
3173.dloc: Front matter, 'Los tonos' > 'Otras restricciones en los tonos' > 'Sílabas con tono ⁵ en la raíz', p. xix; 'Pronunciación del chinanteco' > 'Diferencias de pronunciación', p. xv; 'Introducción', p. xi; Gramática chinanteca sec. 24.1-24.2 'Las palabras tomadas del español', pp. 572-573.
3173.prule: Word stress ('acento fonético', the syllable with the greatest force or emphasis) falls on the root syllable; prefixes and suffixes are added to the root and are unstressed (an unstressed tone-5 prefix dissimilates to tone 4 before a stressed tone-5 root: *ma⁵lie⁵i³ > ma⁴lie⁵i³ 'empezará'). In nouns the root is the final syllable (classifier prefix + root, e.g. o¹to³ 'plátano'), so nouns are stressed on the final = root syllable; in verbs the root is followed by a person suffix (ma⁴-lie⁵-i³), so the stressed root is not word-final. The position is set by morphological structure (root vs. affix), not by syllable count or weight.
3173.srule: Not mentioned in Skinner & Skinner 2000 (front matter 'Pronunciación del chinanteco' p. xv, 'Los tonos' pp. xvi-xx, 'El acento' p. xxi; Gramática sec. 24 pp. 572-573): stress is named once, as the root-syllable 'acento fonético'; nothing on secondary or rhythmic stress.

The only stress-related remark elsewhere concerns Spanish loans and states how Spanish stress is mapped onto tone, not an exception: [p. 572, sec. 24.1] Muchas palabras del español que se introducen al chinanteco que tienen el acento en la penúltima sílab…
3173.tone: Five level tones numbered 1 (alto) to 5 (bajo) plus four contour tones (23 and 34 falling, two rising), fully lexical ('Muchas palabras se distinguen solamente por los tonos que llevan', p. xi; minimal quintuple sei¹/sei²/sei³/sei⁴/sei⁵, p. xvi). Tone processes described: pronoun enclitics realized as tone substitution (hyphen + number, p. xviii-xix), tone-5 dissimilation on unstressed prefixes before a tone-5 root (p. xix), a few adjectives changing tone after certain nouns (p. xix), loan tone mirroring Spanish stress (pp. 572-573). Stress is mentioned only in passing, to define the root as the syllable bearing the 'acento fonético'; nothing on ballistic vs. controlled syllables (orthographic h is a glottal closure; no ballistic marking in this orthography). The section 'El acento' (p. xxi) concerns only the written accent distinguishing bisyllabic úa from the diphthong ua.

tn.quote: Como antes se menciono, el chinanteco de Usila es un idioma tonal. Por medio de numeros volados se indica el tono o las combinaciones de tonos despues de cada silaba de la palabra. Para indicar los tonos sencillos, se emplean los numeros del 1 al 5 . Los tonos asi indicados son: 1 alto 2 semi-alto 3 normal 4 semi-bajo 5 bajo ... Ademas de los cinco tonos sencillos que se pronuncian a nivel, hay cuatro combinaciones de tonos que distinguen palabras. Dos combinaciones son descendentes, o sea, bajan de nivel: 23 ... 34 ... Dos combinaciones son ascendentes, o que suben de nivel: 32 ... 43 ...
tn.translation: As mentioned before, Usila Chinantec is a tonal language. Superscript numbers indicate the tone or the tone combinations after each syllable of the word. To indicate the simple tones, the numbers 1 to 5 are used. The tones so indicated are: 1 high, 2 semi-high, 3 normal, 4 semi-low, 5 low ... Besides the five simple tones, which are pronounced level, there are four tone combinations that distinguish words. Two combinations are falling, i.e. go down in level: 23 ... 34 ... Two combinations are rising, i.e. go up in level: 32 ... 43 ...

3174.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Usui is described as a two-tone language: on each full (major) syllable a lexical contrast between mid-level tone (M, unmarked, ca. 33~22) and falling tone (F, marked with a grave, ca. 31~21), with minimal pairs (ka 'wear sandals' vs. kà 'climb'). The schwa of the prefixal minor syllable (C0ə-) carries no tone and is devoiced or pronounced 'like a neutral tone'; syllables closed by ʔ show no tonal contrast and are always somewhat high; pitch realisation also co-varies with onset voicing; sentence intonation (sharp fall on sentence-final particles, rise at the end of a phonological word, esp. subordinate-clause end) overlays. tn.translation: 2.4 Tone. As tones of Usui we recognise the two kinds shown in (27). (27) a. Mid-level tone (M): unmarked, written V; pronounced at about 33~22. b. Falling tone (F): marked, written V with grave; pronounced at about 31~21. /ə/ bears no tone of its own and is devoiced or pronounced like a neutral tone. Syllables ending in the glottal stop (ʔ) are always pronounced at a somewhat higher pitch and show no tone distinction. Minimal and near-minimal pairs are given in (28): a. ka 'put on sandals' vs. kà 'climb'; b. kãmi 'village' vs. kã̀ 'put on trousers'; c. kaŋ 'be thirsty' vs. kàŋ 'classifier: cloth'.

3178.tone: Venda is a tone language. Meinhof 1901 sec. 40 c (p. 655-656): 'In Bezug auf die Tonhöhe unterscheiden wir hohen und tiefen Ton. Ausserdem giebt es tonlose Silben. Durch die besondern Einflüsse der Töne aufeinander entstehen 4 Töne, die zwischen dem hohen und tiefen Ton liegen, und ein Ton, der über dem hohen Ton liegt' - he separates Tonhöhe (pitch/tone) from Tonstärke (stress) and states a stress rule for the latter, so the record is fixed and quantity-insensitive rather than tone or pitch accent. Modern work: Cassimjee 1983 (H/L autosegmental tonology; contour tones only on penults), Kusmer 2019: 220-221 ('Tshivenḓa does not have lexically contrastive vowel length, but lengthens the penultimate syllable of intonational phrases... The penult of the entire (declarative) utterance is always lengthened'; utterance-internal penult lengthening variable) recasts the penult prominence as phrase-level penultimate lengthening in a tone language and never uses the word 'stress'; Tzanakakis 2019: 52 (after Poulos 1990, Ziervogel et al. 1972): 'syllable stress is not significant, but tone is'.

3179.prule: Penultimate syllable of the surface word (after all phonological rules); non-distinctive except in a few stems with stem-final stress. A word-final vowel 'broken' by a glottal stop (VʔV) counts as two syllables, so stress lands on the vowel before the ʔ (= penult).
3179.srule: Not mentioned in Applegate 1973, sec. 226 'Stress' (ms. p. 2-11; the whole one-page section and neighbouring secs. 224-230 read): the sketch gives one stress per word (penult, or stem-final in a few stems) and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.
